Hack-Nation · Challenge 03 · Agentic Scientific Discovery · Databricks × Omnigent

Fire Lab

An AI lab of 7 agents that learns where to put prescribed burns — and checks whether the answer still holds when the wind changes.

5experiment rounds
19,620fire simulations
13cited papers
11hypotheses tested
32 minquestion → approved recommendation
N

Need

0:08–0:28
  • Fire agencies can treat only ~5% of a landscape a year with prescribed burns.
  • Where matters: doing nothing burns +51.1% more area than even random 5% placement (95% CI [43.1, 61.1]).
  • Each plan needs thousands of fire simulations → analysts compare a handful, one at a time.
  • Hidden risk: a plan tuned for one wind can quietly fail when the wind changes.
Our question

With a fixed 5% budget, which placement rule minimises burned area and homes exposed — and does it still win under a different wind?

Win rule, fixed before any agent ran

≥10% less burned area than random · 95% CI excludes 0 · Holm p < 0.05 · vs no-treatment and random controls on identical fires.

How to read the maps black = treated cells (the 5% budget) green = fuel load (light low → dark high) blue = water (cannot burn) red ring = assets / homes burn maps: black = never burns → yellow = burns most often cyan ring = assets on burn maps white on burn maps = water

Approach

↺ A Director agent (Claude Opus) runs the loop and decides each next step; six Claude Sonnet specialists do the work. They pass record IDs, not prose — every claim traces back to a stored item.
Science guardrails

Fixed 20,000-simulation budget · win rule fixed before any agent ran · no-treatment + random controls in every experiment · held-out ignitions and weather for transfer.

Integrity guardrails

Evidence must cite a real paper (checked on OpenAlex) · results and statistics are written by tools, never typed by a model · hypotheses labelled agent-generated.

Human in the loop

Omnigent policies: budget caps, large experiments and the final recommendation pause for a person to approve.

A

How the lab thought — 5 rounds

0:50–1:15
R1 · screen

6 strategies. Path-centrality (+16.0%) and hybrid (+13.6%) made fires bigger → rejected. Wind strips lead (−26.1%) but p = 0.0509 → confirm, don't promote.

R2 · confirm

Strips built for the SW wind: −29.6% [−37.3, −22.1] ✓. Denser strips did worse.

R3 · transfer

Same plan, NW wind: only −14.5%, Holm p = 0.49 ✗
Transfer test FAILED for the leader … Run one more round (round 4) to find a single FIXED placement that is robust to wind direction. — D3

R4 · new idea

Hypothesis H9: orient strips between the winds (270°). Wins SW −15.3% and NW −31.0% ✓

R5 · stress

Extreme weather: −26.4% [−34.4, −19.5] ✓ → safety review → human approval.

The moment a result changed the plan

Finding F3 (transfer failed) → Decision D3 (new round, new hypothesis) → H9 → the recommended plan. The failure was predicted in advance by hypothesis H5 — the lab tried to falsify its own leader.

It checked its own work

In D1 the director caught the analysis agent reading an efficiency score backwards and corrected the record; the planner wrote 10 rival designs and justified each of the 5 it chose.

Black = treated cells · green = fuel (light low → dark high) · blue = water · red/cyan ring = homes · burn maps: black = never burns → yellow = burns most often. Under NW wind, fire slips past the 225° strips.

B

Benefits — what we found

1:15–1:40
How to read the chart orange = strips built for SW wind (225°) teal = strips built for W wind (270°, recommended) filled = wins · hollow = does not win bar = 95% confidence interval red dashed = −10% bar · grey line = same as random left of 0 = better than random placement
Recommended rule (REC1, human-approved)

Fire-break strips laid across a westerly (270°) wind, 12 cells apart: the only plan that won in all three weather regimes — SW −15.3%, NW −31.0%, extreme −26.4% burned area vs random.

Honest trade-off

Under SW wind it protects homes worse than random (+16.2%, flagged high risk by the safety agent). The SW-tuned plan stays stronger if the wind really is SW.

For a fire planner

11 hypotheses, 7 controlled experiments and a safety review in 32 minutes — every number traceable to a record ID, with negative results kept.

C

Competition — and where we stand

Explains whyyes, slowlynoyes — recorded decisions

Where we lost: on pure single-weather optimisation, random search found sparser strips (spacing 20, ~74% less burned area than no treatment) — our agents never tried spacing > 12. Next experiment: test spacing 16–20 strips for transfer, then a real landscape (LANDFIRE fuels + Cell2Fire).

Appendix · Limitations and what we learned building it

Scientific limits
  • Synthetic 120×120 landscape and a simplified stochastic fire model (no spotting, crown fire, suppression); treated cells are modelled as non-burnable.
  • The 270° idea was proposed after seeing the round-3 failure (risk R7): it needs an independent re-test.
  • Benchmark: agents spent 18,120 sims and never reached the single-weather optimum that random search finds in ~1,080.
  • Outputs are ranked candidate rules for expert review — not burn prescriptions.
Process notes
  • Round-4 runs were sized at 4,500 sims, just under the 5,000-sim approval trigger (the trigger is per call — a policy gap to close).
  • An earlier attempt on an open-weight model (gpt-oss-120b) was discarded: its director wrote evidence under another agent's name and invented a report. Tool-level guards kept fake results out of the record; we switched models and restarted from a clean record.
  • Budget: 19,620 / 20,000 simulations; 8 statistics items; 104 per-plan results.
